newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FORECAST-Bullish NZ market looks for good CPI data.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Bullish NZ market looks for good CPI data.

text.p: New Zealand markets are in bullish spirits ahead of December quarter inflation data on Friday and itching to take interest rates lower, economists said on Monday.

The new target band for underlying inflation, widened in December by the new centre-right coalition government to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent, gives the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) more room to manoeuvre in its fight against inflation.

In December the RBNZ forecast a 0.5 percent rise in December quarter underlying inflation, for a 2.3 percent annual rise. Economists surveyed by Reuters expect on average 0.41 percent, for 2.15 percent annually.

Economists said the wider target band meant markets were considerably more relaxed about the CPI data, after six consecutive quarters of bearish out-turns where inflation was at or above the ceiling of the old 0-2 percent target band.
Annual underlying inflation at 2.3 percent would be inducement enough for a rally in interest rates, even though it is well above the mid-point of the new target band, they said.

"If it comes in in line with the Reserve Bank's forecasts or lower, the market will certainly rally. The market is quite bullish at the moment and seems to be very positive about things, so if it was to come in as expected, even that would set things off," said ANZ Bank senior economist Bernard Hodgetts.

Hodgetts said an annual result of 2.4 percent might spark a small sell-off but it would be muted and reasonably short-lived. "An extra point, while it's not so good, is unlikely to be quite as negative as it was under a narrower target," he said.
ASB economist Anthony Byett agreed that if the annual figure did not exceed 2.3 percent it would be favourably received.

"Conditions now are probably tighter than are required for the inflation outlook...there is scope for easier conditions." The strength of the currency's Trade-Weighted Index, which hit nine-year highs last week, was seen as strengthening the argument for lower rates.

Short term interest rates, currently around 7.55 percent, could push as low as 7.3 percent, but the RBNZ would be wary of the effect on the medium-term outlook for inflation in the non-tradeables sector, Hodgetts said.

"It's unclear how far they'll allow things to go, but I guess if the currency remains up where it is at the moment they really don't have much option if the market does decide to push rates down," he said.
"If they try and underpin rates then possibly the currency will be even firmer."
However, Westpac economist Joselyn Stroombergen said any rally on the back of a figure within 0.2 percent of RBNZ forecasts would be short-lived.

"Given the yearly rate will still be stuck around the 2.2 percent, 2.3 percent level, there are still going to be concerns as to whether or not that's the top and what's going to happen from here on out," she said.
Stroombergen said the 6-12 month inflation outlook was more important than December quarter figures, and pointed to inflationary risks such as government spending and higher minimum wages.

Byett and Hodgetts agreed the inflation outlook for next year was not so rosy, with inflation expectations likely to rise to the top half of the new target band, more social spending on the agenda and tax cuts scheduled for July 1998.

"Really it depends on the Reserve Bank's resolve to do something about it. I'd be reasonably confident that as long as there's no political interference they are likely to remain focused on keeping inflation within the band," Hodgetts said.
"They are likely to go into tightening mode during 1998 if they feel the fiscal situation is a threat."
